## Overview

The constructions of the previous vignettes work for alphabets in any category
with products, not only for finite sets [@CastilloRamirez2026]. Two choices of
category give automata with extra structure that can be put to use:

- In the category of vector spaces over a finite field, the cellular automata
  are the *linear* ones. They compose by multiplying coefficients, so long
  composites are cheap, and whether one can be run backwards is a question of
  linear algebra.
- In the category of partially ordered sets, they are the *monotone* ones.
  They preserve order, so two runs bound every run started between them.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CategoricalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore: CellularAutomataCore, LocalRule, Moore, Life, Torus, CAProblem,
                            solve
using Plots
using Random
using Statistics
```

## Linear cellular automata

Over the field `GF(p)` of integers modulo a prime `p`, a linear cellular
automaton adds up its neighbours with fixed coefficients:
`τ(x)(g) = Σ_s a_s x(s g) mod p`. Elementary rules 90 and 150 are linear over
`GF(2)`, with coefficients one on the two neighbours, or on the two neighbours
and the cell itself:

```{julia}
Z = CyclicGroup(64)
rule90 = LinearCA(Z, [63 => 1, 1 => 1]; p=2)
rule150 = LinearCA(Z, [63 => 1, 0 => 1, 1 => 1]; p=2)
```

They are cellular automata in the general sense too, and agree with the rules
written with exclusive or:

```{julia}
B = FinAlphabet(0:1)
CellularAutomaton(rule90) == CellularAutomaton(Z, [63, 1], p -> xor(p...); dom=B)
```

## Composition is multiplication

A linear automaton is a polynomial in the shifts, and composing two of them
multiplies their polynomials. Squaring rule 90 doubles the distance to its
neighbours, because the cross terms cancel modulo 2. So rule 90 applied
`2^k` times reads only the two cells at distance `2^k`:

```{julia}
[k => sort(collect(keys(coefficients(rule90^(2^k))))) for k in 1:4]
```

Powers are computed by repeated squaring, so even a thousand steps cost a few
multiplications. On a ring of 4096 cells, rule 90 applied 1000 times reads
`2^6 = 64` cells, one for each way of choosing a subset of the six ones in the
binary digits of 1000, as Lucas's theorem predicts:

```{julia}
big = LinearCA(CyclicGroup(4096), [4095 => 1, 1 => 1]; p=2)
(length(coefficients(big^1000)), 2^count_ones(1000))
```

The general composition of local rules cannot do this: its composite local
rule calls the original once for every path through the memory sets, a number
that doubles with every application. Composing the general rule 90 with
itself ten times and evaluating it on one configuration:

```{julia}
x = Configuration(Z, rand(Xoshiro(1), 0:1, 64))
general90 = CellularAutomaton(rule90)
(general90^10)(x);
(rule90^10)(x);
linear_time = @elapsed (rule90^10)(x)
general_time = @elapsed (general90^10)(x)
(same=(rule90^10)(x) == (general90^10)(x), slower_by=round(Int, general_time / linear_time))
```

The two give the same configuration, and the general composite is hundreds of
times slower already at ten steps.

## Other primes

Over `GF(3)` the cells take three values. The rule that adds a cell to its two
neighbours modulo 3 draws a different fractal from a single seed:

```{julia}
Z3 = CyclicGroup(81)
sum3 = LinearCA(Z3, [80 => 1, 0 => 1, 1 => 1]; p=3)
seed = Configuration(Z3, [g == 40 ? 1 : 0 for g in 0:80])
rows = [parent(seed)]
for _ in 1:40
    push!(rows, parent(sum3(Configuration(Z3, rows[end]))))
end
heatmap(0:80, 0:40, permutedims(reduce(hcat, rows)); c=[:white, :steelblue, :darkred],
        yflip=true, colorbar=false, xlabel="cell", ylabel="time", size=(700, 360))
```

## Running backwards

A linear automaton is a bijection of configurations exactly when its matrix is
invertible over `GF(p)`, and then its inverse is linear too. Rule 90 is never
invertible on a ring, since the configuration of all ones and the
configuration of all zeros both go to all zeros. Rule 150 is invertible on a
ring of `n` cells exactly when 3 does not divide `n`. These are the ring sizes
from 3 to 12 on which it is invertible:

```{julia}
rule150_on(n) = LinearCA(CyclicGroup(n), [n - 1 => 1, 0 => 1, 1 => 1]; p=2)
filter(n -> isinvertible(rule150_on(n)), 3:12)'
```

On a ring of 10 cells, the inverse undoes thirty steps:

```{julia}
L = rule150_on(10)
back = inv(L)
x0 = Configuration(CyclicGroup(10), rand(Xoshiro(2), 0:1, 10))
(back^30)((L^30)(x0)) == x0
```

## Monotone cellular automata

When the states are ordered, a monotone rule is one where raising the state of
any cell it reads never lowers its result. Then a configuration that is
everywhere at least as high as another stays so under the automaton, step
after step. A pest that spreads to a plant with at least two infested
neighbours among its eight, and never leaves, is monotone; Life is not, since
a crowded cell dies:

```{julia}
spread = LocalRule(Moore(1)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    return cell == 1 || count(==(1), nbrs) >= 2 ? Int8(1) : Int8(0)
end
B8 = FinAlphabet(Int8[0, 1])
(spread=is_monotone(CellularAutomaton(spread, Torus(60, 60); alphabet=B8)),
 life=is_monotone(CellularAutomaton(Life(), Torus(60, 60); alphabet=B8)))
```

## Bounding an uncertain survey

A survey of a 60 × 60 field confirms some infested plants and flags others as
possibly infested. The true state lies between the confirmed map and the
confirmed-or-flagged map. Because the spread rule is monotone, running those
two maps gives a lower and an upper bound on every scenario in between, at
every step, without running the scenarios:

```{julia}
rng = Xoshiro(3)
confirmed = Int8.(rand(rng, 60, 60) .< 0.03)
flagged = Int8.((rand(rng, 60, 60) .< 0.05) .& (confirmed .== 0))
lower = solve(CAProblem(spread, confirmed, 20))
upper = solve(CAProblem(spread, confirmed .+ flagged, 20))
scenarios = map(1:20) do _
    truth = confirmed .+ Int8.(flagged .& (rand(rng, 60, 60) .< 0.5))
    return solve(CAProblem(spread, truth, 20))
end
all(all(lower.u[t] .<= s.u[t] .<= upper.u[t]) for s in scenarios, t in eachindex(lower.u))
```

```{julia}
infested(sol) = [mean(u) for u in sol.u]
plot(lower.t, infested(lower); fillrange=infested(upper), fillalpha=0.2, lw=2,
     label="bounds from the survey", c=:darkred, xlabel="step",
     ylabel="fraction of plants infested", legend=:topleft)
plot!(upper.t, infested(upper); lw=2, label=nothing, c=:darkred)
for (k, s) in enumerate(scenarios)
    plot!(s.t, infested(s); c=:grey, alpha=0.5, label=k == 1 ? "scenarios" : nothing)
end
current()
```

The bounds hold for the whole map, cell by cell, not only for the fraction
infested. Life gives no such guarantee: among random pairs of configurations
on a 6 × 6 torus, one everywhere at least as high as the other, almost every
pair has images that are not ordered:

```{julia}
life = CellularAutomaton(Life(), Torus(6, 6); alphabet=B8)
T6 = TorusGroup(6, 6)
pairs = map(1:200) do _
    a = Int8.(rand(rng, 6, 6) .< 0.3)
    b = max.(a, Int8.(rand(rng, 6, 6) .< 0.2))
    return Configuration(T6, a), Configuration(T6, b)
end
count(((a, b),) -> !all(parent(life(a)) .<= parent(life(b))), pairs)
```
